newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh defense questions key government witness.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh defense questions key government witness.

text.p: The lawyer for accused bomber Timothy McVeigh laced into a key prosecution witness on Wednesday but she stuck to her testimony that McVeigh told her he wanted to destroy the Oklahoma City federal building in an act of revenge against the government.
Witness Lori Fortier, speaking in a quiet monotone, withstood an insistent cross-examination that challenged her credibility and motives for testifying.
As she spoke, McVeigh stared at her from the defence table, expressionless.

Chief defence attorney Stephen Jones reminded Fortier of her admitted drug use, blasted her for accepting immunity from prosecution and asked whether she was telling the truth now or when she issued earlier public statements that McVeigh was innocent of the bombing.
He also accused her of testifying against McVeigh to stay out of jail and of trying to sell her story. "I never wanted to sell my story," Fortier said.

Her testimony on Tuesday and Wednesday was the most incriminating so far against the 29-year-old Gulf war veteran who is accused of planting the huge bomb that destroyed the Alfred P. Murrah federal building and killed 168 people on April 19, 1995.

Fortier, the wife of McVeigh's Army buddy Michael Fortier, said McVeigh tried to recruit her husband into helping him bomb the federal building when he visited her trailer home before the explosion because he wanted to avenge the deadly FBI 1993 assault on the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas.

Michael Fortier has entered into a plea agreement, admitting he knew McVeigh had planned the bombing but did nothing to stop it. Michael Fortier is in federal custody, facing up to 23 years in prison and is also expected to testify for the prosecution.

Jones hinted that Lori Fortier's drug use may have affected her recollections. "I wasn't on speed when he came and told us this," she responded, referring to McVeigh's stated plans to bomb the federal building.

Jones asked very specific details about a time Fortier and McVeigh were alone together -- and her husband was away at work -- when McVeigh used soup cans to illustrate the mechanics of his planned bomb.
"Was that the only thing you were doing with Mr. McVeigh?" Jones asked, and she answered, "Yes."

She testified she could not believe McVeigh would carry through on the plans. But when asked specifically by Jones "Did you take him seriously, yes or no?" she answered "yes" because she had seen him making preparations.
But she immediately added that because McVeigh was a friend, "I didn't want to believe he was capable of this."
Jones, seeking to damage her credibility, asked Fortier if she felt responsible for the deadly attack.
"All you had to do to prevent the death of 168 people was to pick up the telephone?" he asked.
"Yes," she said.
"And you didn't," Jones said.
"Yes," she said in a weak voice.
Jones also tried to intimate that Fortier had been extensively coached, especially by lead prosecutor Joe Hartzler, whom she referred to by his first name in the courtroom three times.

She testified that she said McVeigh was innocent soon after the bombing because she was afraid of being linked to the attack, she feared for herself and her family and she wanted to avoid media attention.
"At the time we were lying about everything to everyone," she said.

The 24-year-old mother of two denied that prosecutors gave her a list of questions they would ask her or was advised by the government how to dress in court. But she admitted to undergoing two "mock" cross examinations in which Hartzler played the role of the defence attorney.

The day's testimony ended with a mining engineer, who delivered a primer, complete with charts and drawings, on how ammonium nitrate and fuel oil explosives work and where such ingredients can be purchased. Further technical testimony was expected when the trial was scheduled to resume on Thursday.
